Oliver Fame"

"I know him—he was among the shark
fighters—a very fine young fellow. Still,
I don't quite understand why they should
prefer him to the other"

I think he is a better man. I like Amyas,

he has many good qualities; but, to tell the

truth, he does not inspire me with implicit
confidence. He is ambitious and master-
ful, and, fear, not always sincere"

preferred Oliver, Amyas would refuse to
accept their decision."

"I think it is very likely"

strife, perhaps bloodshed, all which my

return would of course prevent. While we
were afloat I did not think about it. My
mind was too full of other things; it never
occurred to me that we should be cast
away so far from home, and in circum-
stances which would make it appear that
we had perished. But now I see clearly

back with all possible speed. But we shall
gain rather than lose by delaying our de-
parture until tomorrow morning. And
are you not taking the matter rather too
seriously? We shall be back in two or
three days—at the outside in four—and in
that time no great harm can be done.
They will surely seek for us; because the
Diana has disappeared, it does not follow
that we are all drowned, and Amyas could
not decently—"

Here I pulled up short, for a startling

suspicion had flashed suddenly into my
mind, an idea to which I hesitated to give

utterance.

"Well," said Nab, "what were you go-
ing to say?"

sure Amyas would not take any steps

he would not attempt to assume the protec-
torate till he had assured himself that
you were not living"

"That is not what you were going to
say!" she exclaimed, imperiously. "Tell
me at once; I insist on knowing!"

thoughts, Queen Nab," answered, quiet-
ly. "Suppose I admit that you are right,
that I was going to say something else,

how are you to know that I am telling you

my real thoughts, after all? I may tell
you something else"

"But you will tell me your real thoughts,
Mr. Erie. You have right to be offend-
ed. I was too absolute; insisted when I
ought to have besought. Tell me frankly
what was in your mind. You may be sure
I shall not abuse your confidence, and I

will give you mine"

She spoke softly, almost caressingly; and
when Nab lowered her voice, it was sin-
gularly sweet and musical. I had already
half resolved to "speak out" and even if

I had not, it would hardly have been pos-
sible to refuse a request so graciously
made.

"Well, my thought was this—it came
unbidden—take it for what it is worth;"

LONDON, January 19.-The Grand Old
Man must have slept the sweet placid sleep
of babyhood last night, for just before he
had crawled into his bed in Naples tele-
gram came to tell him of a knock-down
blow to the Tories and a humping victory
for Gladstone, Parnell, home rule and vir-
tue in general Govan is a Scotch district,
and the Tories fondly hoped it was theirs
for good and all. They not only carried it
at the Parliamentary election in 1886, but
also in 1885, when Gladstone was supposed
to be strongest This morning the Tory
landlord and his mugwump Unionist
brother had their day spoiled by the news
that Yesterdays election had replaced the
Tory majority of 362 by home rule ma
jority of 1,071.


The attempts of the Tory press to wriggle
out OF the crushing defeat are more humor-
Gus than usual, and go to swell the pleasant
sensation of the Home Rulers, the magnitude
OF whose victory surprises them almost as
much as it does the Tories. The only re-
source of the latter is to roundly abuse poor
Sir John Fender, their defeated candidate,
as unfit for the place, nice. gentlemanly
habit which, by the way, is rather charac-





whom we hear SO much about.


WHAT THIS ELECTION MEANS.


This is the most significant of all the bye
elections. 1t means, in plain English and
beyond all doubt, that in the present state
of public opinion, general election would
mean a tremendous victory for Grand Old
Gladstone, and a chance for the Irish to
manage their own national affairs.


A hon
such as must have tremendously excited any
other big town, has just been witnessed here,
and London seems scarcely to have noticed
1t. / mean the substitution of the County
Council for the corrupt Board of Works,
which ran things before. The Importance
of this change lies in the fact that London
is now threatened with a government in the
interests of the masses of its inhabitants,
and not of its proprietors. The change is a
Tory measure, but it looks very much as
though the Tories would very soon find in
Mr.. Ritchie, with his local government bill,
a dark-complexioned Frankenstein of a
most obnoxious type.


The Grand Old Man didn't fight the BILL
a fact which some complained of, but it will
soon be seen that on that occasion Gladstone
proved himself foxy as well as grand and
old. He allowed the Tories freely to legis-
late themselves into very hot water.


ENOUGH TO FRET THE TORIES.


Gu: of 119 county Councillors, 20 or more
are ultra-Radicals, who are pledged to such
measures as are calculated to make the
head of the average Tory look infinitely
more fretful than the back of the most cas-
lily irritated porcupine. These 20 Council
lors, if they are true to their colors, will
fight to take the control of the police awav
from the Home Secretary; to tax ground
rents-a very painful thing for the Tory
land owners; Inappropriate the endowments
of turtle-eating city companies-a painful
thing for big-bodied business magnates; to
have water, gas and tramway companies
controlled by the city; to have the public
admitted to the meetings of the Council,
and to effect numerous other gravely revo-
lutionary and common sense reforms.


The Council is queer body, with none
of the uniformity of character observed in
the traditional Board of Works or Alder
manic body. Lord Roseberry, who is as
radical as any lord married to a Rothschild
can very we'll be, is a member, and will
probably be President of the Council Lady
Sandhurst and Miss Golden, daughter of
the anti-protection celebrity have both been
elected, but while women are allowed to
vote, it is not quite settled whether they can |

Man must have slept the sweet placid sleep
of babyhood last night, for just before he
had crawled into his bed in Naples tele-
gram came to tell him of a knock-down
blow to the Tories and a humping victory
for Gladstone, Parnell, home rule and vir-
tue in general. Govan is a Scotch district,
and the Tories fondly hoped it was theirs
for good and all. They not only carried it
at the Parliamentary election in 1886, but
also in 1885, when Gladstone was supposed
to be strongest. This morning the Tory
landlord and his mugwump Unionist
brother had their day spoiled by the news
that yesterday's election had replaced the
Tory majority of 362 by home rule ma-
jority of 1,071.


The attempts of the Tory press to wriggle
out of the crushing defeat are more humor-
ous than usual, and go to swell the pleasant
sensation of the Home Rulers, the magnitude
of whose victory surprises them almost as
much as it does the Tories. The only re-
source of the latter is to roundly abuse poor
Sir John Fender, their defeated candidate,
as unfit for the place, a nice gentlemanly
habit which, by the way, is rather charac-
teristic of the man whom we hear so much about.


WHAT THIS ELECTION MEANS.


This is the most significant of all the bye
elections. It means, in plain English and
beyond all doubt, that in the present state
of public opinion, a general election would
mean a tremendous victory for Grand Old
Gladstone, and a chance for the Irish to
manage their own national affairs.


A honour such as must have tremendously excited any
other big town, has just been witnessed here,
and London seems scarcely to have noticed
it. It means the substitution of the County
Council for the corrupt Board of Works,
which ran things before. The importance
of this change lies in the fact that London
is now threatened with a government in the
interests of the masses of its inhabitants,
and not of its proprietors. The change is a
Tory measure, but it looks very much as
though the Tories would very soon find in
Mr. Ritchie, with his local government bill,

and White that the Supreme Court decision
in favor of wholesalers, bottlers and brew
ers throws open the doors to food of in
temperance and free liquor. The charming
unconventionality of the "speak-easy"

dead. But Judge Stoves session yesterday
dispelled that brief illusion. = Heavy fines

stopped, it is not clear that the increase in
the number of wholesalers, or bottlers, or
brewers can work any material enlargement
of the traffic, or multiply disorder in the
consumption.

law will continue need not be doubted.

nizing the competition of unlicensed places,
and the public desire that high license get
a full and fair trial, the "speak-easy" can
soon be accounted thing of the past.

some idea of the topography, resources,


wealth, etc. of the northern counties. In con-


versation with a clever looking gentleman, I
asked him:


"What county do you live in?" "Santa
Rosa," he answered. "Can you raise oranges
successfully that high up?" "No sir. What
do you raise!" "Pine trees." "I presume
you are a saw-mill man?" "Yes sir. What
about?" "They are not going to give out." "How
so!" "I've go over and cut off the biggest trees, and when we get back others have
grown large enough to cut." "Where is your
market?" "The world, out by the Gulf of
Mexico." "I suppose your high, dry, piney
we had to kill a man to start a graveyard."


Soon after that the wires were found to be
down and the train had to stop at Pensacola
junction about three hours to learn that all
was right ahead and safe to run on. About
midnight the Santa Rosa gentleman and I
were standing talking, when a rotund and ru-
bicund old man came walking up to us, un-
wrapping at the same time buckskin string
from around a metallic plate about an inch
and a half in diameter, and asked "Are either
of you gentlemen troubled with liver complaint, dyspepsia, neuralgia, rheumatism or
anything? If so, by simply wearing this bat-
tery you will soon be entirely relieved." "Will
it cure anything and everything!" I asked him.
"You see what it has done for me," he said,
spreading himself out before us in the mean
time. The Santa Rosa gentleman spoke up
and said "We don't need any remedy for
any kind of sickness in our country." "Where
is that, pray? I'd like to go there myself!" said the metallic-plate and buckskin-string
man. "Santa Rosa county," the gentleman
answered. "Why, I'm just from there!" said
the ruddy man. "Then you've been labouring
under a mistake," remarked I, "in supposing
that it was your so-called battery that had
brought you here; it must have been the salu-
brious climate of Santa Rosa." "But I only
stayed there a month," he retorted. "So much
the more in favor of that healthful country!"
"If it did so much for you in one month, how
long, sure enough, might not a man reasona-
bly expect to live there before being called
upon to go and help make up a graveyard?"


The discomfited old man walked away
wrapping the buckskin string around his me-
talic humbuggery.


All across the northern portion of the State
of Florida I saw but little, if anything else,
to live but health. The most of the land
that I saw didn't even have pine trees—it
couldn't even produce blackjack oaks. I was
told there were better lands on either side of
the ridge on which we were running. That
may possibly be so, but I can't say.


When I saw the sanitary conditions in and
around Jacksonville I didn't wonder they were
fever scourged there last year. But for the
purifying and health laden breezes fresh from
the proximate Atlantic Ocean the inhabitants
would have been desolated long ago. And if
there be not mighty clearing up inside and
outside of that city they may be fever strick-
en any summer.


I left home for Indian River, which lies
along the Atlantic Ocean on the southeastern
coast of Florida, and thither I undeviatingly
wended my way. But, when I got there, I
could hardly see the river for the water—it
being three or four miles wide with uniformly
low banks. But I reckon there is no part of
earth more healthful and pleasant than some
parts of that river; and there are some en-
chanting localities along its shores—beauti-
ful beyond description. It would require
more space and word-painting than you can
afford me at this advanced stage in the ac-
count of my trip; I may attempt descrip-
tion, if desired, in another article and also an
account of the orange business, &c. The
current price of land in those charming local
valleys is $1,000.00 per acre. There are cheaper
lands however, but not so favorably situated
nor so desirable in every respect.


I have travelled a great deal in the States
and out of them; but this was my 10th
visit to Florida. And the more I see of the
States and countries, the more I think of
Louisiana, which I verily believe is the best
of all for general purposes.


Placemine, March 20, '89. D. W. FOSTER

Los ANGELES, January 5.—Mr. Osgoodby, author of the famous Murchison letter, whose identity was revealed yesterday, says he did not, until few days before the correspondence was made public, have any conception of its importance in political sense. Bell, it was determined to make the letters public and on the 10th of October the letters were brought to Los Angeles by Bell, acting for Osgoodby.

health, and feel like a laborer of Saturday
evening returning home with his weeks'
work done and his weeks' wages in his pocket,
and glad that tomorrow is the Sabbath.
Just about three years ago, while lectur-
ing in New England, a message came from
under the sea bidding me to hasten and
take commission to relieve Emin Pasha
at Wadelai; but as people generally do
with faithful pack horses, a number of little
trifles, odds and ends are piled on over
and above the proper burden. Twenty
various little commissions were added
to the principal, each requiring due care
and thought. Well, looking back over
what has been accomplished, I see no reason
for any heart's discomfort. We can say we
shirked no task, and that good will, aided
by steady effort, enabled us to complete
every little job as well as circumstances
permitted. Over and above the happy end
ing of our appointed duties, we have not
been unfortunate in geographical dis-
coveries. The Aruwimi is now known from
its source to its bourn.


THE GREAT CONGO FOREST.


"The great Congo forest, covering as
large an area as France and the Iberian
peninsula, we can now certify to be an ab-
soluta.
this time, beyond the least doubt, have been
located, and Ruwenzori, the Cloud King
robed in eternal snow, has been seen and its
flanks explored and some of its shoulders
assessed, Mounts Gordon Bennett and
Mackinnon Cohes being but giant sentinels
warding off the approach to the inner area
of the Cloud King.


On the southeast of the range connec-
tion between Albert Edward Nyanza and
Albert Nyanza has been discovered and the
extent of the former lake is now known for
the first time. Range after range of mountains has been traversed, separated by such
tracts of pasture land as would make your
cowboys out west mad with envy, and right
under the burning equator we have fed on
blackberries and bilberries, and quenched
our thirst with crystal water fresh from
snow beds. We have also been able to add
nearly 5000 square miles of water to Vic-
toria Nyanza.


"Our naturalist will expatiate upon new
species of animals, birds and plants he has
discovered.


Our surgeon will tell what he knows of
the climate and its amenities. It will take
us all we know how to say what new store
of knowledge has been gathered from this
unsearched field of discovery. I always
suspected that in the central regions be-
tween the equatorial lakes something worth
seeing would be found, but was not pre-
pared for such harvest of new facts.


ECLIPSED ALL HIS PAST EXPERIENCE.


"This has certainly been the most extraor-
dinary expedition I have ever led into
Africa. A veritable divinity seems to have
hedged us while we journeyed. I say it
with all reverence. It has impelled us
whither it would, effected its own will, but
nevertheless guided and protected us. What
can you make of this, for instance? On
Aug. 11, 1887, all the officers of the rear
column are united at Yambuya. They have
my letter of instructions before
them, but instead of preparing for the
morrow's march to follow our trail, they
decide to wait at Yambuya, which deci-
sion was made during the most awful
season any community of men ever en-
dured in Africa or elsewhere. The results
are that three-quarters of their force die of
slow poison. Their commander is murdered
and the second officer dies soon after of


wasted to skeleton and obliged to return
home. A fourth is sent to wander aimlessly
up and down the Congo, and the survivor
is found in such a fearful pest hole
that we dare not describe its horrors.
On the same date, fifteen miles
away, the officer of the day leads
thirty-three men of the advanced column
into the bush, loses his path, and all con-
sciousness of his whereabouts, and every
step he takes only leads him further astray.
His people become frantic, his white com-
panions, vexed and irritated by sense of
the evil around them, cannot devise any
expedient to relieve him.

"They are surrounded by cannibals, and
poison typhoid arrows thin their number.
Meantime, in command of the river
column, am anxiously searching up and
down the river in four different directions,
though at first my scouts are seeking for
them, but not until the sixth day was
successful in finding them.

in 1888, a year later, on Aug. 11, I listen

viving officer of the rear column at
Banalya and am told of nothing but death and
disaster, disaster and death. I see nothing but horrible forms of men smitten
with disease, bloated, disfigured and
scared. Our camp,
famous for the murder of poor Bartellotte,
barely four weeks before, is simply sicken-
ing. On the same day, 600 miles west of
this camp Jameson, worn out with fatigue,
sickness and sorrow, breathes his last.


"On the next day Aug. 12, 600 miles east,
Emin Pasha and my Officer Jephson, are

who menace them with loaded rifles and
instant death, but fortunately they relent

three to desist. The news was brought
by Capt. Alger, of the American sealing
schooner Alger, who arrived on
the steamer Olympian from Port Townsend.
The captain, in an interview,
said: July 30 We were in Behring
Sea, about fifty miles west of St. Paul,
when we sighted the cutter Rush steam-
ing up to us on our quarter. We at once
hove to. Some minutes afterward a boat
put off from the Rush, and Lieut. Tuttle
boarded us. He asked for my pa-
pers, which I at once handed him, and
after perusing them he proceeded with
two men to search the ship. He didn't
find anything, however, though that is
not to say there was nothing to find
aboard. After coming up out of the hold
when he had finished searching the
ship I said to him: Well, what luck
have you had in the search? He said: I
will tell you. On the 11th of July we
captured the Black Diamond and went
board to take charge of her. On the 23d
of July we sighted the schooner Minnie.
Her owner, Capt. Jacobson, was aboard
at the time, and she had 543 seals. We
took possession of her, and dispatched
her to Sitka, also. Yesterday, 18th
of July, we bore down on the Pathfinder
and found 500 sealskins aboard of
her. We put another man on board and
ordered her off to Sitka as well. Last week
we boarded both the Arctic and there
say they also had some skins aboard
but let them go, as they had been too
long caught, but ordered them out of the
sea. After telling me this the lieu-ten-
ant told me I had better get out of the
sea at once, and was then pulled aboard
the steamer, which headed for the
east. We then set sail for the south,
and arrived Monday at Neah bay. I
then left my schooner there and came
up from Cape Flattery to Port Townsend.
I caught the Olympian and just reached
Victoria. My schooner will, I expect,
be on the road to Seattle now. I leave
here on the Olympian to-day to join her.
Excitement prevails in this city.
Both schooners are well known here
and their catch is a very valuable one.

Capt. Alger sighted first the Minnie and
then the Pathfinder, each with one man
as a prize crew on board. Both signaled
their intention of not long to stay at all,
but of coming to Victoria, so that
within twenty-four hours they may be
expected in the harbor. When Lieut.
Tuttle went aboard the Alger several of
his sailors expressed themselves as
heartily sick of their work.

The weather was delightful, and the exhibitors were as busy as possible preparing their displays for the multitudes that are confidently expected to be in attendance to-morrow and on each succeeding day until the close on Friday night. There were great many visitors to the GROUNDS, but no one would admit that the fair was really in operation, the opening being simply an assurance of the events that will follow.

With a continuance of fair weather there is no doubt that this will be the most successful fair in the history of the association. During the year many important improvements have been made on the grounds which are now in better condition than ever before. Long famous as a stock-breeding county, Butler in the exhibits of her stock raisers this year surpasses all previous records. Last year the association was cramped for room, and the stock and cattle shows to some extent encroached upon the track and domain of the trotters, while largely interfering with the privileges of the boothkeepers. Ample provision is made this year, three large new buildings having been erected for the accommodation of the stock in the large space at the rear of the enclosure. The association gives its most earnest efforts to the accommodation of the exhibitors yet the interests of the trotting men have not been overlooked; their stable space has been enlarged, and the grandstand has been extended sufficiently to guarantee the fullest accommodation to the lovers of horse racing.

There were two events on the card yesterday, neither of them very important, yet of sufficient interest to entertain the people who were on hand to begin with the fair at the beginning. The first race, in the 2-year-old class, had four entries and while the time made was not very fast, the racing was earnest enough to be exciting. There were four entries to interest the spectators until the close, the result being anything but foregone conclusion.

PLENTY OF SPORT.

There will be good sport on the track to-morrow, the programme including three races. These events are the three-minute race, the 2:30 pacing event and the race for stations. There have been ten nominations made for each one of these and it is believed that none of the entries will be drawn. There are some flyers among the PACERS, and the stations race is expected to be of unusual interest. On Thursday there will be 2:40 trotting event, the race for the Farmers cup and the free-for-all. For each of these large fields have been entered, speedy animals from many sections of the Western part of the State being upon the ground to participate, and the day bids fair to be one of the liveliest of the season on the track.

The fair will close on Friday when the free-for-all pace, the $50 trot and race for 4-year-olds will be decided. In the stables of the sporting men are trotters from New Castle, Beaver, Allegheny, Pittsburg, Sandy Lake, Evansburg, Kittanning and other places, the trotters and pacers numbering in all over 20. There is a noticeable improvement in the general features of the fair. The various exhibits will not only be more numerous this year than ever before, but they will also, in nearly every case, be of higher grade. This characteristic of the displays is conspicuous, especially in the exhibition of agricultural implements and in the main Exposition building where there is an array of furniture, pianos, and other kinds that would be creditable, even to the big Exposition in Pittsburg. The floral display is also notable, but Butler must resign the credit of that feature to Allegheny, the exhibitors being Ludwig and Richter, of that city. In the fine art department the exhibition is the finest ever made here, and to the esthetic this will probably prove the most attractive feature of the fair.

The foreshadowed success of the fair is undoubtedly due to the judiciously liberal management of the association in the arrangement of their premium list, and in their guaranteed protection of exhibitors and purchasers of privileges. An abundance of means for wholesome amusement have been provided but the fraudulent 'fakir' has been frowned upon and excluded from the fair grounds and its vicinity.

ALWAYS THERE.

The striking machine is here, of course, and so is the lemonade fiend, and his friend, the peanut vender. So is the fellow who gives you cane, if you succeed in passing ring over it, and near him is freak show with monstrosities enough for twice the price of admission, for those who like that sort of thing.

The list of premiums is extraordinarily long, and unusually liberal. Among its most important features is the educational department, in which the pupils of the schools of the county take the liveliest interest. In the contest for prizes the lists are open to all pupils. The inducements held out to aspiring competitors are shown in the following list of awards:

MAPS.—Best map of North America by pupil in primary grade—Copy of Youth's Companion for one year. Second best—Copy of Harper's Young People. Best map of South America by pupil in primary grade—Copy of Youth's Companion for one year. Second best—Copy of Harper's Young People. Best map of Europe by pupil in primary grade—Copy of Youth's Companion for one year. Second best—Copy of Harper's Young People. Best map of South America by pupil in grammar school grade—Copy of Youth's Companion for one year. Second best—Copy of Harper's Young People.

EXAMINATION PAPERS.—Best set examination papers by pupil in Third Reader—"Madam How I Lost My Head" and "Lady Why" — Kingsley. Second best—"Aunt Martha's Cupboard" Kirby. Best set examination papers by pupil in Fourth Reader—"In New Grenada" Kingston. Second best—"On the Banks of the Amazon" Kingston. Best set examination papers by pupils in Fifth Reader—Dickens Child's History of England. Second best—Copy of Ben Hur, by Wallace.

PENMANSHIP.—Best specimen of penmanship—Gold pen. Second best—Gold pen. Best specimen penmanship by pupil 16 years or older—Fountain pen. Second best—Fountain pen.

DRAWING.—Best specimen free hand drawing by pupil 12 years or younger—Set of drawing instruments. Second best—Set of drawing pencils.

AN INTERESTING FEATURE.

It goes without saying that the work of the pupils is one of the most interesting exhibits of the fair, and it is bound to enjoy a lion's share of the attention of the thousands of visitors. The variety and extent of the general exposition may be inferred from the fact that the exhibits are divided into 12 classes, the ensemble being as complete and comprehensive as it is possible to make it.

In large numbers the stock and cattle show will be the features of chief interest. In this department, the display will be finer than ever before made in this county. It includes among the heavy draft horses breeds of the Clydesdale, English Shire, Percheron, graded Percheron and Cleveland bays, light draft and trodden horses, roadsters and carriage horses; in all these grades there are especially fine representatives on view, and the Judges will have no sinecure in awarding the prizes.

The cattle show embraces Durhams, Dexters, Jerseys, Holsteins, Ayreshires, Guernseys, Herefords, Aberdeen, Angus, Galloway, all registered, also unregistered Durhams and Jerseys, beside native grades and milk cows. The sheep show embraces Merinos, South Downs, Cotswolds, Leicesters, Oxforddowns, Lincolnshires, Hampshires, Shropshires, Downs, all registered, and crosses and grades. Among the swine are creditable representatives of Poland China, Berkshire, Yorkshire, Jersey Reds, Essex, Cheshire and Chester White, all registered. The poultry show is also very complete, embracing representatives of all the most famous strains.

because impossible as it may seem in the nineteenth

He had tried such means of self-sacrifice as ap-

when it was the rage, but he did not catch fever,
lose his life nobly rescuing someone from anything

with whom he worked showed signs of falling in
love with him, so he gave up dueling as

He had tried politics, choosing an unpropitious

did not find even that successful as a means of
self-sacrifice, for his colleagues simply worshipped
him, and none of his old friends made the least
difference in their behaviour toward him. Some

Whelan was still only half recalled from his
own castle-building. "All right; do you want
anything?" he said.

"Yes, I want—generosity."

Davis would rather have said "justice," but
some instructive knowledge of his friend's char-

to get what he wanted if he called it by the more
attractive name.

To be just is only one's duty; that is why one so
seldom does it; but there is something flattering
to one's vanity in the mere name of generosity.

Whelan was thoroughly interested now. "Are
you in some trouble?" he said. "I can help
you. Come into the Mall and let me hear."

They walked along slowly in the shadow of
the trees, silent at first but presently Davis be-

you have and how little I have. I want YOU to
recognize that and be
generous."

warmly, "but I know what friendship is, and I
shall not fail you. Speak without any more
preface; what form is this generosity to take?"

 Much yet remains to be accom- plished in electric condition but the great gains of the closing year, tech nical and commercial, are abundantly apparent.

 The rate at which electric motors have been installed for stationary power is scarcely less noticeable than the development of electric traction during the year. About the first of September it was estimated that 5000 electric motors were driving machin- cry in the United States. A thousand have probably been added since. It seems reasonable to estimate the num- Der put in operation for the year at not much less than 4,000.

 The use of the storage battery as means of distribution may fairly be said to have made relatively slow ad- vancement, while in many special cases it's employment has been of great value and importance. Its problems have had and continue to enlist the close att tention and skill of many able in- vestigators and inventors, and it can not be doubted that the modern suc- cess thus far attained by this obvious ly important and necessary means of distributing electricity will be followed not long hence by such Improvements as will make the accumulation a general and trustworthy instrument in cleo trical engineering.

 The electric light, arc and incan- descent, has become so familiar to every body, even in the far Western Territories, that its continued rapid spread no longer attracts attention. It is expected everywhere; its absence in any considerable town is more noticed than its presence. Great activity in the installation of central station plants has prevailed during the year, especial ly in incandescent lighting. The suc- cess of the alternating current method of distribution in covering large areas of relatively sparse consumption has largely stimulated the demand for electric lighting in the smaller towns of the country, and has also con- tributed not a little toward in- citing the companies whose business is based upon other methods of distri- button to improving the capacity of their apparatus and the serviceable- ness of their lamps. The life of lamps has been materially prolonged, while reduction has been effected in the amount of energy required per candle power. Whatever may bepthought of the policy of competition in prices, there can be no question of the gener- al benefit of competition in the eff ciency and trustworthiness of appara- tus and lamps. Competition of the former kind, while severe, has crip- pied only the weak, while that of the latter sort has resulted in advantage to both producers and consumers.

 The practical success of the employ ment of alternating currents has re- acted in the laboratories of scientific research, and led to the study of new questions, or old questions in a new light-study and experiment which have already done much to clear the path of the practical electrician in his work, and which indicate the early ac- quisition of further electrical knowl- edge of great significance.

 The years scientific and practical advances are great enough for con- graduation, but not great enough to induce complacent satisfaction and re- taxation of effort. Electrical Engineer.

Last week while Hon. John, Ex-Governor of Kansas, was in New York, he was interviewed on the tariff question, and upon being asked what he had to say upon said question, replied

"Our whole tariff system is wrong in principle, because it imposes its burdens upon what we consume, instead of what we possess, thus compelling the poor day-labourer to carry a great financial load on the necessities of life, (which rich and poor alike are compelled to have) as is carried by the man who is worth his millions. All financial burdens placed by our Government upon the people should be measured, not by their capacity to consume, but by their ability to pay. A man who has $4,000 and no children is justly entitled to pay ten times more protection than should be paid by the man of only $1,000 and ten children; but under our present tariff system the poor man, with ten children, pays ten times more taxes than is placed upon his more prosperous and well-to-do neighbor. In other words, the burden is placed upon the number of children, and not upon the number of dollars possessed."

"What remedy would you propose for this injustice to the poor?" inquired the reporter.

"Why, I would restore to the people what I believe to be God-given right, that is, to trade anywhere in this wide world where they can buy the cheapest, without being compelled, as they now are, to pay tribute to a favored few."

The so-called Conservative party had been in power, but the last elections returned a sweeping Liberal majority. The Governor knowing that his tenure once depended upon his recognition of the popular will began making appropriate changes in various offices, displacing Conservatives and appointing Liberals. He did this on only a small scale and gradually. But the Conservatives were unwilling to relinquish their hold upon the offices. First they demanded that he should make no changes whatever. Then, when he disregarded their clamor they began to agitate for his removal, holding meetings for the purpose and sending petitions to the Sultan. The petitions were disregarded at Constantinople, and then the Conservatives began to demand union with Greece. They introduced resolutions to that effect into the Legislature. It was overwhelmingly rejected. Then they resorted to violence; killing or wounding the successful Liberals, manning their cattle, destroying their crops and burning their houses. The Liberals, of course, retaliated; the police, too, sides some with one, some with the other party, and now the unhappy island is divided into two warring factions: the barefoots and the haversacks. Between the two there is often open and deadly conflict, always implacable antagonism. No barefoot will speak to haversacks, or enter the same cafe or church with him. No barefoot judge will condemn a fellow barefoot for any crime committed against haversacks, nor will a haversack policeman arrest a fellow haversack for any offence against a barefoot. Justice is suspended. Business is at standstill. Society is chaos.

In this wretched strife there is no division between creeds or nationalities. Christians and Mahometans, Greeks and Turks, are to be found on both sides. It is simply a fight between the in and the out. The Greek Government, through its Consuls, has used its influence for peace, but in vain. It has emphatically discouraged the demand for annexation, but the hot-headed agitators reply that Crete shall be annexed to Greece whether Greece is willing or not. Up to this time the Turkish Government has acted with its customary irresolution. It has not only neglected to use the necessary energy to restore order, but it has not even allowed the Governor to do so. That officer had at his command troops sufficient to quell all the disturbances in a day. But the garrisons were strictly required not to fight, to make no single move unless they were themselves attacked. The Governor has now been recalled, and through the efforts of the commission there is hope of a peaceful settlement of the Cretan troubles.

WASHINGTON, May 14.-The senate at
its last session appointed a committee to
investigate the question of the irriga-
tion and reclamation of arid lands, con-
sisting of Senators Stewart, of Nevada;
Plumb, of Kansas; Allison, of Iowa;
Hiscock, of New York; German,
Jones, of Arkansas. The committee
will commence their work on the first
of August next, starting from st. Paul,
MINI. They expect to spend ten weeks
in the field, and will visit Northern Da-
kota, Montana. Idaho (as far as the
Snake river basin), Utah. Nevada. Cali
fornia, Arizona, Southwestern Texas,
along the valley of the Rio Grande from
Ell Paso to San Antonio; thence by the
Fort w Orth, Santa Fe & Colorado rail-
road, across the Staked Plains, the
Pan Handle region and part of South
eastern New Mexico; through that terri
tory to Southwest Kansas, Colorado and
Wyoming. The committee will be ac-
companied by Maj. Powell, director of
the geological survey. Richard j. Hin
ton, who prepared for the department
of agriculture report on Irrigation
in the United States,'' published by the
United States senate in 1887, accom-.
panies the special committee as expert,
having been appointed irrigation engi-
neer in the United States geologi-
cal survey. The United States geo.
logical survey will have six engineer
ing parties in the field some time be-
fore the committee starts. The public
domain west of the Tooth meridian will
be divided finally into about fifteen hy-
biological districts, as the topography
of the region best indicates the proper
storage basins. The six districts now
formed embrace the region between the
Tooth meridian west longitude and the
Rocky Mountains, Montana, Idaho,
Utah, Nevada and all the basin section
east of the Sierras, California, west
thereof and New Mexico and Arizona.


Nothing Dangerous.

Pixley is suffering from pneumonia.
She was unable to perform last night.
The attack is pronounced slight. She
is expected to be around again within
week.

SAN Francisco, September 12th.-Argu-
ment in the Nagle case was resumed this
morning in the United States Circuit Court
before Judges Sawyer and Sabin. There
was fair attendance of spectators.


Attorney Wilson was the first to address
the Court this morning. He said that
whenever question arises relative to juris-
diction there was mode provided whereby
it could be changed from State Courts to
Federal, and vice versa. The system of ex-
changing is constitutional and harmonious.


Mr.. Wilson continued in his argument
at great length, citing many cases wherein
had the facts been tested in connection
with jurisdiction it would have been found
that the Federal Courts could have tried
the cases as well as the State Courts. Con-
gress has passed an Act which says that its
servants shall act in protective spirit.
These Acts of the Federal Government
were passed after the Civil War. They
were passed for protecting the nation's
powers, and they were all based on the
same line and carry the same weight.


QUESTION OF POWER.


The Attorney General has power over
the United States Marshals, and the is no
doubt but that he issued instructions to the
United States Marshal of this district look
ing to to the proper protection of the per-
son of Justice Field. Discretion is neces-
sary, and it was no doubt exercised. We
contend that the prisoner was justified in
his act. No act committed by a United
States officer in the performance of his duty
is crime. The prisoner saved the life of
Justice Field as well as his own. He fred
the fatal shot only at the last extremity.
He is justified in law and reason, and we
ask this Court to dismiss him from custody.
He has committed no crime. He should
not be sent to Stockton for trial.


STATE JURISDICTION.


Mr.. Wilson was followed by District At
torney White, of San Joaquin county, who
argued in behalf of the jurisdiction of the
State. He cited case after case showing
that the Federal Court should turn Nagle
over to be tried by that tribunal. If the
prisoner is innocent, why should the Fed
eral Court desire to try him? Who will
prosecute him in that Court? Not the Dis
trict Attorney, for he has been retained on
the side of the defense under orders from
the Attorney-General. The prisoner was
not serving warrant or carrying out the
contents of one. The crime was committed
on State soil, and Nagle should be tried by
State Court. The prisoner had no power
greater than private citizen, since he was
not, as stated before, serving a warrant or
carrying out the contents of one. The
crime was not committed on Federal soil
and we ask that this Court turn him over
so that he may be tried by State tribunal.
With this request we submit the case.


Nothing further was done and the Court
adjourned until tomorrow.

THE TRAVELS OF A NOVICE JOURNALIST


PUBLISHER.


To the Editor of THE Tribune.


Sir: The search for the North Pole has its difficulties. Bondsmen are often hard to find; Stanley's whereabouts are not positively discovered. Our friend Japhet searching for his father unknowingly was sorely hindered. But all these are like being carried to the skies on honey bees, easily compared with a search for a publisher.


One morning I awoke with the consciousness that I should be up and doing in order to gather a few shekels to grease the wheels of my conveyance. My evil genius, a punishment for many misdeeds, suggested that I try literary work, and ignorance was perfect bliss with me—I followed his advice. I wrote a little article on a prominent man whom I knew well and gave it to my cousin to take downtown with a venture of his own in the same line. They were left with a big newspaper, and for three weeks waited patiently for news. Then, armed with the courage of despair, I resolved to seek the Great Unknown. Arrived at the editor's room, saw a bell knob, and rang. When the door opened and an urchin appeared I nervously blurted out, "The editor?" "Your card!" demanded the youth. I had not intended to make calls so I had none with me, but I meekly gave my name instead. "Which one do you want?" This was awful. I stammered: "Oh, any of him!" for I had only prepared myself to deal with one. The youth heaved himself away, and I sat down on a chair without a seat and struggled to gain composure, wondering if a dozen or two editors would come out and ask me which one I wanted.


A lady who has written for twenty years told me she was only fourteen when she started out to dispose of her first story, and four big brothers had done their best to frighten her by horror tales and frequent mention of the black and grinning youth they call the devil. However, she persevered, and went up to the rooms of the little village where she tapped softly, and when a young man with long and lanky locks opened the door, she could only gasp out, "Are you the devil?"


My break was not nearly so bad. I rehearsed my little speech while waiting. At last the Editor was announced and I rose and stammered, "You have had a little article of mine for three weeks and I am very anxious to know if it is accepted." "What was your article on?" I only gave the title and he left me. This Editor was simply like the other men I had met in everyday life and I grew at my ease. He returned with the MS in his hand and told me he thought they would use it. "I would so much rather you would give it back to me," I said, "than keep it on an uncertainty, for hope deferred, you know." "Yes, I know; I have been through the mill myself. You will see all this in either next Sunday's issue or the Sunday following." I thanked him and mustered courage to inquire if he would read a story if I sent it to the paper. "Why, certainly! We always read everything sent as a matter of duty." That was sarcasm; I did not recognize it, as it was in my ignorant mind, but later I have wondered if it were not absurd on its face for any reasonable person to believe. Another article which had with me this editor suggested I take to another paper which he named. This place was harder to get into. There was nothing but a long narrow hall with a flight of stairs and a sign pointing to the further end. At the end was the elevator, "Editorial rooms," said I to the man. We went up till the roof stopped us and I was told to walk to the end of the hall, turn to the south-southwest, up a flight of stairs, turn to the north-northeast, go down three steps, up another flight of stairs, turn to the left and go to the further end of the hall. I followed instructions wondering if the Signal Service had towers on the building. At the last step I found myself in a large room opening into several small ones. An elderly gentleman half rose to greet me; he was annoyed that a woman could have found him without special instruction. "I am Dan of the Sackbut," I commenced, "thought you might use this short story." "I think you must want Mr. Blank in the next room," he said. Now, to my ignorant eyes there were three Mr. Blanks in that room, so I stood in the doorway sizing them up and chose the wrong man, to whom I handed my story. After a careless glance he murmured, "This is for you, Dr. Blank." Mr. Blank looked at it and said, "If we do not use it we will return it." "I can call for it to-morrow and save you the trouble," meekly said I. "You need not trouble yourself madam; your address is here." So he took up his pen and considered myself dismissed. That night I sent dimes worth of stamps for postage and at intervals of three weeks wrote a note, but never have heard from my story.


As I stepped from the building into the street I readily wondered why I had not met some of that, oh, the army of the condemned carrying their crosses in the shape of rejected manuscripts. Having received another MS, I concluded to take it to another newspaper, so I walked into that one and demanded the editor. Three doors to the right and around the corner across the street, and up two flights of stairs. Really, I thought, it certainly cannot do divinity that doth hedge around the various editors, but most assuredly they might well be secured in an assault by unknown persons. However, I passed three doors, etc., and knocked on a door and waited on it. No response; I gently turned the knob and encountered the gaze of two young men in short sleeves. "I have a story which would like to know if you can use it." "The editor is in the next room." Accordingly into the next room I went. Here was another man, not so young, in a coat and waistcoat. "I also have an article here; I would like to know if you can use it." "He is in the next room," continued my journey. On entering the third room I saw a man more undressed, with neither coat nor waistcoat, but a white shirt on. I mentally said, "It must be the right one; he won't dare to go any further." So that was the man at last, and I said my business. "I have a story that would return tomorrow if not an immediate return is necessary." I began to think as I declined, that as this chief also had been in haste, my second visit perhaps had been in vain. I trust the heaven's angels feared to tread and resolved to act those mails thereafter. Still these gentlemen are sending authors of poetry and prose—as much as I am really able to make out. Hence an editor is sorry for them; it appears to me as rather a sort of pillar of rubber or core of some symbolic place as a target for the mob to pelt with stones. He said, "They may be soft as they may be—no matter, they strike the impression, but it is momentary." The pillar is still in good shape for now.

Brooklyn, Feb. 10, 1889

There IS a familiar story ABOUT how Daniel Webster, when he was practising law IN New Hampshire, loudly denounced a quotation from a textbook made by a rival attorney as absurd and untenable, upon which the opposing lawyer quietly explained that the passage so contemptuously treated had been introduced into the volume from one OF Lord Mansfield's decisions, that great jurist's exact language being preserved. The following anecdote about a famous old character In Whitley County, Ky. has much the same flavor. Joshua Barnett was a WASP and a religious orator, and possessed a prodigious memory. The "Jellico News" tells the story:


"Uncle Josh, as he was generally called, had an appointment to preach Sunday at Out-of-the-way schoolhouse in his neighbourhood and two noted lights of a rival denomination attended the meeting for the purpose OF criticizing the sermon. One was named Jones, the other Waterman. Uncle Josh, who, it appears, was aware of their intentions, concluded to checkmate them, and instead of preaching a sermon he began repeating from memory, and without any comment whatever, one OF the Epistles of St. Paul for nearly an hour, chapter after chapter, fell from his lips, accompanied by grave and doctrinaire &c. nature and information. Brother Jones, at the end OF some thirty minutes, arose with disapproval written all over his face, retired from the house and took seat in the yard upon a bare and PROSTRATE tree which was used as a horse-block. Brother Waterman stood it some ten minutes longer, when he too joined Brother Jones. Well, Brother Waterman, what do you think OF such sermons? said Brother Jones. I think, said Brother Waterman, why, I think if the good Lord will forgive me this time for listening to such rotten doctrine, I will never be guilty again."

Great Engineering Feats Performed Many
Centuries Ago.
Tho very first thing done by every
community, savage or civilized, is to
provide for water supply. Savages
simplify matters by placing their tene-
ments within easy reach of river or
lake. Civilized people have their
water brought to them. This is not of
easy accomplishment, and some of the
greatest feats of engineering have been
performed in supplying water to
ancient and modern cities.


When the British captured India,
they found. in all parts of the country,
tanks and reservoirs on an enormous
scale, and some of them a thousand
years old.


The water works of Peru were even
older. The Incas built aqueducts from
the slope of the Andes, for distance
of more than one hundred miles. to the
capital. The water was carried part
ly through tunnels cut in the rocks and
partly on arcades on supporting pillars
of mason work to span valleys, the
channels being composed of cut stone
without cement. From these great
aqueducts a number of branch canals
and conduits were laid laterally for
irrigation purposes.


The ancient water works at Jerusa
lem consisted first of wells in the lime
stone ridges on which the city was
built; but as the population increased,
tanks and cisterns for rain water were
placed ia secure Enclosures and within
the walls of the temple. An aqueduct
of stone laid in cement was construct
ed to bring water from the pools of
Bethlehem, about six miles distant
Strabo mentions that it was a very rare
occurrence for Jerusalem to suffer from
water famine


About the year 600 B. c., Polycrates,
King of Samos, built an aqueduct to
supply his capital, bringing water
through a tunnel cut through limestone
rock for a distance of six thousand
yards. About the same time, the peo-
pie of Lycia, in Asia Minor, carried
water across the vale of Petrea through
a stone syphon


Carthage brought water from the hill
ranges on the south, over seventy miles
distant. and the ruins of an ancient
aqueduct may still be seen.


The water works of Athens were be-
gun about $50 b c., and consisted of
stone aqueducts lined with baked clay,
and carried alsnost wholly on the sur
face of the ground


The ancient city of Mexico was sup
piled with water through a wooden
aqueduct, built by Montezuma. carried
across a causeway. In Egypt and
China, gigantic works for conveying
water have been in existence from re-
mote antiquity. Taken all in all, the
efforts of the mcderns are yet insignifi-
cant compared with those of the
ancients.-G0lden DaVs.

built; but as the population increased,

placed in secure enclosures and within
the walls of the temple. An aqueduct
of stone laid in cement was constructed to bring water from the pools of

Strabo mentions that it was a very rare
occurrence for Jerusalem to suffer from
water famine.


About the year 600 B.C., Polycrates,
King of Samos, built an aqueduct to
supply his capital, bringing water
through a tunnel cut through limestone
rock for a distance of six thousand
yards. About the same time, the people of Lycia, in Asia Minor, carried
water across the vale of Petrea through
a stone syphon.


Carthage brought water from the hill
ranges on the south, over seventy miles
distant, and the ruins of an ancient
aqueduct may still be seen.


The water works of Athens were begun about 550 B.C., and consisted of
stone aqueducts lined with baked clay,
and carried almost wholly on the surface of the ground.


The ancient city of Mexico was supplied with water through a wooden
aqueduct, built by Montezuma, carried
across a causeway. In Egypt and
China, gigantic works for conveying
water have been in existence from remote antiquity. Taken all in all, the
efforts of the moderns are yet insignificant compared with those of the
ancients.—Golden Days.

In the brilliant pageantry of a public parade of the Knights Templar, one of the striking features of the triennial conclaves, the marching of large bodies of men with military precision and their marching in orderly lines to the inspiring strains of martial music is a spectacle sufficient to attract crowds of admiring spectators. When, in addition, the uniforms are handsome and striking, with sufficient variety in color to avoid monotony, the spectacular effects are complete. The Knights Templar parade combine all these features and not only on the day of the parade, but on all the days that the visitors will throng the streets of the city, the Knights Templar uniform will be a familiar sight. It will be interesting to give some account of the origin of the present uniform. It may be said the present form is the outcome of a great deal of legislation on the part of the Grand Encampment.


THE EARLY COSTUME


In the early days of Knight Templary the dress adopted was picturesque, but rather unsuitable to the needs of modern duties of Knights Templar. It was as follows:


white woolen mantel to reach the knee in front, and taper away to the ankle behind fastened with white cord and tassel, and with a red cross pattée on the left shoulder; white woolen tunic reaching to about three or four inches above the knee, with the cross upon the left breast; white stock, with falling white shirt collar; tight white pantaloons; bush boots with pan tops turned over five inches broad, no tassels; spurs gilt, with red feathers; sash of white silk, half yard in breadth, tied in a knot in front, the ends edged with white silk fringe hanging down and small red cross near the extremities; white woolen cap with red leather band; or, if he has obtained a diploma from the Grand Master, a red velvet cap; no feather; cross-hilted sword with brass guard, and white ivory hilt; scabbard of red morocco; belt of red leather, with gilt buckle; tan gauntlets, with red cross on the wrist; badge, and enameled black cross, with white orle, and small red cross enameled thereon, suspended from the neck by a red ribbon with white edges, about two inches broad, passing through the ring of the badge.


CHANGE MADE.


Subsequently a more practicable dress was adopted. The suit was black, with black gloves, black velvet sash, trimmed with silver lace, crossed the body from the left shoulder to the right hip, having at its end a cross-hilted dagger. A Maltese cross at the end where the sash crossed the left breast was a nine pointed star in silver, with a cross and serpent of gold in the center, within a circle, around which were the words "In hoc signo vinces." The apron was of black velvet, in triangular form, and edged with silver lace. On its flap was a sacred triangle of silver, perforated with twelve holes, with cross and serpent in the center. On the center of the apron a skull and cross-bones between three stars of seven points. The belt was black, to which was attached a cross-hilted sword. The caps varied in form and decoration in different encampments.


THE ORDER OF 1854


Another alteration was made in 1862, when the Grand Encampment of the United States directed that the dress should consist of a black frock coat and pantaloons, with white scarf and sword belt and white gauntlets. Finally, at the Chicago conclave, it was directed that the coat should be cut military fashion, and that the buttons should be of gilt. The order has not, however, been very strictly followed. There is still a lack of complete uniformity. Some Commanderies have retained the cape and apron, others have varied the shape of the hat, and others again have not deemed it essential that their coats should be of precise military fashion.


THE LOCAL COMMANDERIES


All the Commanderies in this District, with the exception of Washington, No. 1, wear the uniform with white sash and belt and no apron. No. 1, however, still retains what is known as the "black uniform." They have adhered to this uniform in spite of the order of the Grand Encampment to the contrary. When the delegates attended the Grand Encampment in 1874 at New Orleans they were forbidden to wear this uniform. They all went to New Orleans, however, headed by the late Henry Z. Stansbury, and, while they did not wear the prescribed uniforms, they carried them along in their trunks. The matter was brought up in the sessions of the Grand Encampment, and, after a long discussion, a resolution was adopted permitting certain Commanderies, No. 1 being among the number, to wear this uniform. As soon as this decision was reached, the forbidden uniforms appeared from their hiding places and the members of No. 1 walked about the streets of New Orleans in triumph displaying the then celebrated "black uniform." The Knight Templar dress may be described as severe military in character; the different parts of the uniform have no Templar significance, but Templar symbols are introduced as ornaments and also to give character to the uniform.

those most familiar with plowing,
is that this necessary farm operation is
performed solely for the purpose of
making the soil looser. The plow GER
tainly does to some extent break up the
clods, but generally it leaves them too
loose, and the farmer must cultivate or
drag the surface to recompact it and
make good seed bed. Sod ground must
necessarily be plowed so as to turn un-
der the grass, but it is equally import
ant after plowingto harrow the surface,
or the roots will send up new shoots
and quickly become a meadow. For
some kinds of crops following a naked
stubble, mo deep plowing is needed.
We have known good winter wheat
grown by cultivation that did not even
turn under the stubble. but only har-
rowed the surface enough to have it
comparatively level. The wheat roots
in such cases spread out horizontally
near the surface, because the undis-
turbed soil beneath is not prepared to
receive them. Frosts mellow the un


dersoil, and when spring comes the
roots strike down, the plant spreads and
makes good crop. With deeper fall
tillage, most of the wheat would be
winter-killed.--Americam Cultiudtor.

A long lost brother, who was supposed
to be dead, and on whose estate letters of
administration were granted to his sister
by Surrogate Rollings, of New York, in
February, 1887, has turned up alive and
healthy. Surrogate Ransom has revoked
the letters, and the property, largely in
creased through his sisters careful man.
agement, has been restored to the man
whose supposed death she had mourned.
His name is Pierre E. Beauron, and his
sister is Marie F. Jodrey. He was born
in Switzerland forty-six years ago and
came to this country when he was seven
years old. He lived in Shohola, Pa,
until 1868, when he started for Havana.
He lived there three years, then started
for the Pacific coast, and few months
later departed for Rio Janeiro, where he
remained eighteen months. He next
went to India and lived there four years.
From there he went to Australia, where
he lived nine years. Then he proceeded
to Europe and remainedin France seven
months and in Spain seven months more.
For over seven years prior to his return
to Shohola his sister had not heard of
him.-Butfalo News.

would play until they had won enough to go
to America or they would lose all. And if
they lost all they would die together and
leave their friends no further trouble about
them.

They were here few days only in Monte Car-
lo. They risked their louis only for a short
time, and they spent the remainder of the
days and evenings in strolling about the
mantle terraces and quiet pathways of the
beautiful gardens, whispering together of
love and looking into each other's eyes.

The end came quickly. One evening they
went up in the soft moonlight to the fairy
land of Monte Carlo. They entered the
Casino. They had come to their last few
golden coins. One by one the croupier's
remorseless rake swept them away and
then the lovers went out of the crowded
rooms, out from the glare of the chan-
deliers and swinging lamps into the tender
moonlight again. Down the "Staircase of
Fortune" arm in arm they went along the
glorious marble terraces that look upon the
sea—on to where at the foot of the great
rock on which Monaco stands there lies the
Corniche. It was their last walk together.
The lovers were going home to die.

That night, in some way which was not
able to ascertain, the guilty and ruined man
and woman obtained some charcoal and got
it into their bedroom. They then closed the
windows and doors and prepared for death.
They wrote a letter—a letter which an
official assured me was so touching that, as
he read it in the room where they lay dead,
the tears ran down his cheeks. Then the
girl—she was but a girl—dressed herself in
snowy white and placed in her breast a sweet
bouquet of violets. Then the charcoal was
lighted and the lovers laid themselves out
for death, side by side, and passed dreamily
into sleep, from sleep to death; and from
death to Judgment.

story. I have told it simply as it hap-

It looks to me though the strike in the Roslyn coal mines has been settled for some time to come, and we shall probably hear of few disturbances in the future at that point. The company was no doubt out of patience at the long-drawn-out uneasiness which prevailed at the mines, and in using somewhat heroic methods to settle the trouble they appear to have had the sympathy of the community in general. The Roslyn strike, like a number of others which have been recorded as occurring at different localities in Western Washington, seems to have been ill advised, and was the outgrowth of dissensions stirred up by vicious and irresponsible agitators. These men exert their influence altogether too often in our mining camps, and most of the troubles which have unfortunately broken out within the last year are to be attributed to their misguided efforts.

It may almost be termed lapse misfortune to have our mines shut down and our miners cease work just at this particular juncture in the history of coal mining. The industry is now growing perhaps more than any other in the territory. Old mines are being furnished with the latest and most approved patterns of machinery and the output increased, new mines are being opened and the coal making a name for itself; and any unsettled differences between employers and employees cannot fail to make progress uncertain and retard the development of our coal interests in every locality. Several mines were shut down during the past summer so that the output was far below what it should have been. Some of the companies were more or less embarrassed in filing their contracts, and the miners by remaining idle were using up any little surplus they might have accumulated and running the chances of reducing themselves to actual destitution.

If labor should remain in that uncertain and unsatisfactory condition for prolonged period, it would necessarily bring about state of demoralization everywhere in coal mining regions. No company will make any effort to increase the output, to enlarge and improve its machinery and to facilitate generally the better working of property if it is continually at war with its workmen, and the fact that there is constant irritation between the two factions representing the employer and the employed must necessarily render coal mining an uncertain field in which to invest money and have tendency to keep away that capital which would otherwise be utilized in developing our vast and yet unopened coal deposits.

No doubt, at times, the miners have just cause for making complaints, but more frequently their grievances are nothing more nor less than the formulated fancy of small but vicious element which is found in every camp, and which, mindful of the real welfare of the miners, attempts to run matters with high hand, make demands which at heart the majority do not assent to, and arbitrarily dictate as to how the end shall be gained. The influence of such men is invariably bad, and listening to their counsels invariably results disastrously to the miner. Their mistaken notions and foolish promptings have brought about so much unnecessary trouble; however, that their day seems to be nearing its close, and it is not unlikely that the honest laborers in our mines will have more regard for their own interests and not be led blindly into disputes and differences which would never exist but for the evil advice of idle agitators. If the miners have real grievances and manfully seek to have them redressed they can rely on the general public to back them, and with public sentiment in their favor there is every probability of their petitions being listened to and justice being granted. But whenever they allow themselves to be led by unscrupulous ringleaders and arbitrarily make demands which in ordinary trade or business would be regarded as unreasonable; whenever the basis of any strike or disturbance is wrong and evidently brought about by few men who are never easy unless in hot water, then the miners' right to support will have been forfeited and in the long run they are certain to suffer for it.

French savant, NJ. Pouchet. This
gentleman selected five well-known
works of different ages, from the
present back to the time of Lucian,
and ascertained the number of color
epithets in each. The general con-
clusion he arrives at is that the
writer always shows marked tend
ency to describe red things, not be-
cause, as has been supposed, our an
cestors were unable to see blue and
its allied shades, but because they
followed the natural tendency to
describe what was prominent. Blue
in nature is not very CONSPICUOUS,
and yellow, though more common in
flowers, has a tendency to lose its
individuality IN Wilderness; but red
is so conspicuous because of its con-
trast to green, which is the prepond-
Grating color in nature. Moreover,
as red is the color of blood, is the
symbol of fire, and is most sought
after in dyes, it soon acquired
moral and intellectual prominence
which would lead to its frequent
mention.

"Say, rather, that the time was sadly and foolishly wasted."


"Are you aware that you have been outrageously robbed?"


"Well, what else could I expect? A person who does not know how to take care of his own should not complain if it is taken from him."


"The tradesmen with whom you have dealt have presented absurd bills. The people from whom you have borrowed money have charged you interest at the rate of 50 per cent."


"Well, that is the business of usurers."


"However, it is necessary to make them disgorge."


"By what means can I do so?"


"You might appeal to their conscience."


"Conscience is a coin that is not current among them."


"Suppose we try to move them."


"We would have our labor for our pains. Indeed, I do not know who they are."


"I will enlighten you. They are Pierre, myself, and a third person, who is the most guilty of us all. I soon perceived (and Pierre, who is a far-seeing person, was of the same opinion) that it would be impossible to arrest you in your extravagant course, carried away as you were by the ador of youth. We determined, therefore, to limit your prodigality by every means in our power. Tradesmen, counting the risk they run with young men of wealth, who let their money slip through their fingers, greatly increase the amounts of the bill they send them. It was arranged, however, with those with whom you have dealt, that, in consideration of being paid at a certain time, the amount of their claims should not be unreasonable. You went into debt, and it became necessary for you to borrow money, and Pierre, in whom you have had blind confidence, undertook to obtain it for you. At this point the third accomplice comes on the scene. This person was very exacting and took mortgages on your possessions which were hypothetical for their full value. It has been ascertained, however, after a careful examination of the schedules of your indebtedness, that you have really spent money at a very reasonable price for the experience you have acquired. Your assets, therefore, amount to about 250,000 francs. The person in question has taken advantage of your carelessness and ignorance of business affairs. I think, however, that an arrangement can be made by appealing to her sense of fairness."


The baron was astonished.


"You know this person, then?" he asked.


"Yes, and you also. Your creditor, your usurer, is Jeanne Rosel."


The young girl had entered noiselessly and overheard this conversation. She approached the three men, saying:


"Yes, Paul, it was I. During these years of foolish dissipation I have never lost sight of you. I knew that, though you yielded at times to wrong impulses, your heart was right, and that when your reason returned you would again be the same Paul as of old, with whom I have so often talked in this room. I was able, with my father's consent, to use the fortune left me by my mother as I saw fit, and in what manner I have employed it you know. You will not be pressed for payment."


"Suppose I insist on immediate payment for the full face of the mortgage."


"Well, perhaps M. Planter can make some useful suggestion."


"A marriage contract is the best means I can suggest of getting you out of your embarrassment," said the notary, smiling.


"Oh, Jeanne!" said the baron, "you have reopened for me the heaven which I thought was closed against me forever. How can I ever repay you?"


Old Pierre, who had been a silent spectator during this scene, the end of which he foresaw, approached his master and said:


"I told you, monsieur, that I would never leave you."


"Ah, you are a monster of dissimulation!" exclaimed the baron, laughing.


At that moment the door of the dining room was thrown open. A delicious odor rose from the steaming soup tureen, and the table glittered with the old family silver.


"Paul," said M. de Rosel, gayly, "give your arm to your wife."


Paul and Jeanne led the way, and the others followed the happy couple.
